key_terms.meaning: Code segment that accesses shared data and must run under mutual exclusion.
Result depends on the timing and interleaving of concurrent accesses to shared data.
At most one process executes in its critical section at a time.
If no process is in its critical section and some want entry, the choice cannot be postponed indefinitely.
A process waiting to enter cannot be overtaken infinitely many times.
Two-process software lock using flag[] and turn variables.
Hardware operation such as test-and-set that reads and updates a word indivisibly.
Lock with acquire and release operations and one owner.
Integer with atomic wait and signal operations used for exclusion or ordering.
Semaphore over an unrestricted range that counts available units of a resource.
Lock where a waiting thread loops checking the lock instead of blocking.
Module combining shared data and procedures with implicit mutual exclusion.
Monitor wait queue with wait and signal used to wait for a condition.
Set of processes each waiting for a resource held by another in the set.
Closed chain of processes each holding a resource needed by the next.
Process holds at least one resource and waits for more.
Design rules that make at least one necessary condition impossible.
Order in which all processes can finish using current and future available resources.
Avoidance algorithm that grants a request only if a safe sequence remains.
Algorithm that finds a cycle or a set of processes that cannot finish.

takeaways: A race condition occurs when interleaved accesses change the result; the critical-section problem is to stop that for shared data.
A correct critical-section solution must satisfy mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.
Peterson's solution is a two-process software protocol using flags and turn; it is mainly of conceptual value on modern hardware.
Hardware atomic instructions such as test-and-set provide the primitive on which mutex locks and semaphores are built.
A mutex has one owner; a semaphore is a counter with atomic wait and signal and can also order events.
Monitors bundle shared data and operations and use condition variables to wait without busy spinning.
Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait together; prevention removes one condition.
Avoidance grants requests only if a safe sequence remains; detection finds cycles and recovery kills processes or preempts resources.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask you to explain the three critical-section requirements, use semaphores or monitors in code, and classify deadlock handling into prevention, avoidance, detection and recovery.

bank.q: Explain the critical-section problem. State and explain mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting with an example of a lost update.
outline: Define race condition and critical section
Show two processes interleaving a read-modify-write and losing an update
State the three requirements with one-line meaning
Give one valid entry/exit protocol outline

bank.q: Compare a mutex lock and a binary semaphore. Why does a mutex have an owner but a semaphore does not?
outline: Define mutex acquire/release and ownership
Define binary semaphore wait/signal with value 0 or 1
Compare blocking, ownership and use for ordering
Give one use case for each

bank.q: Explain a monitor and a condition variable. How does a waiting process avoid busy spinning inside a monitor?
outline: Define monitor with shared data and procedures
State implicit mutual exclusion
Explain condition variable wait and signal
Explain release of monitor lock while waiting and reacquisition on wakeup

bank.q: State the four necessary conditions for deadlock and give one example of each in a resource-allocation setting.
outline: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait
One concrete example for each condition

bank.q: Differentiate deadlock prevention, deadlock avoidance, deadlock detection and recovery. Give one method under each heading.
outline: Prevention breaks a necessary condition
Avoidance uses safe-state or resource-allocation-graph checks
Detection searches for cycles or unfinished sets
Recovery ends processes or preempts resources
One method per heading

bank.q: Write Peterson's two-process solution. Show that it satisfies mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.
outline: Show flag[] and turn variables
Show entry protocol and exit protocol
Prove mutual exclusion by contradiction on turn and flag
Argue progress and bounded waiting for two processes
Mention assumptions about atomic loads and stores

bank.q: Use semaphores to enforce the order A then B: process P1 prints A and process P2 prints B, with B printed only after A. Give the initial value and wait/signal calls.
outline: Declare one semaphore with initial value 0
P1 prints A then signals
P2 waits then prints B
Explain why the order is guaranteed
State that semaphore operations are atomic

bank.q: Given processes holding and requesting resources, draw the resource-allocation graph and decide whether a deadlock exists. Explain the role of cycles.
outline: Draw process nodes, resource nodes and request/assignment edges
Find a cycle
State that a cycle is necessary but not sufficient when resources have multiple instances
Decide deadlock from the graph and process states

bank.q: Apply the banker's algorithm to a given allocation, maximum and available matrix. Find a safe sequence, or show that a request must be denied.
outline: Compute need = max minus allocation
Show work and finish vector step by step
Produce a safe sequence if one exists
For a request, check request ≤ need and request ≤ available
Pretend allocation, run safety check, grant or deny

bank.q: A program uses a shared Boolean busy flag with a plain test-and-set written in C. Find the race and repair it using an atomic hardware instruction.
outline: Show the non-atomic test-then-set window
Explain how two processes can both enter
Use test-and-set or compare-and-swap atomically
Add bounded-waiting logic or a lock queue
State why compiler and CPU reordering matter

bank.q: Compare a spinlock and a blocking mutex for a short critical section on a multiprocessor and for a long critical section on a uniprocessor. Recommend one in each case.
outline: Define spinlock busy waiting and blocking mutex sleep/wakeup
Short multiprocessor section: spin may avoid context-switch cost
Long section: blocking avoids wasted CPU
Uniprocessor: spinning can be useless without preemption
Recommendation with reason

bank.q: A system has all four deadlock conditions. Evaluate which condition is least practical to break in a general-purpose operating system and why.
outline: Review each condition and its prevention method
Mutual exclusion hard for non-shareable devices
Hold and wait needs requesting all resources at once, hurting utilization
No preemption needs preemptible resources
Circular wait needs global ordering and is often practical
Choose least practical with justification

bank.q: Design a deadlock detection and recovery policy for a batch system and for an interactive system. Evaluate victim selection and starvation risk.
outline: Choose detection frequency and cost trade-off
Use wait-for graph or allocation matrix
Recovery by process termination or resource preemption
Batch may tolerate less frequent checks; interactive needs low latency
Victim selection: priority, work done, resources held
Rollback and starvation prevention by age or bounded retries

bank.q: Compare a monitor with semaphores for solving a bounded-buffer problem. Discuss correctness, readability and the risk of signal/wait mistakes.
outline: Show semaphore solution with mutex and counting semaphores
Show monitor solution with condition variables notFull and notEmpty
Compare implicit lock in monitor with manual wait/signal
Discuss missed signal, wrong order and deadlock risks
Conclude with maintainability and common textbook use

bank.q: Explain the system model for deadlock with resource types, instances, request, assignment and release. Why is starvation different from deadlock?
outline: Define resource type and number of instances
Define request, assignment and release edges
Draw or describe a resource-allocation graph
Deadlock is a waiting cycle; starvation is indefinite postponement without a cycle
Give one example of each

glossary.def: The part of a program that accesses shared data and must not run concurrently with another process's critical section for the same data.
A situation where the final result depends on the order in which concurrent operations happen.
The guarantee that at most one process is inside a given critical section at any time.
The guarantee that a process trying to enter an idle critical section will not be blocked forever by processes outside it.
The guarantee that there is a finite limit on how many times other processes may enter before a waiting process gets its turn.
A scheduling or resource policy that can take a resource away from a running process.
A policy where a process keeps a resource until it releases it voluntarily.
A race where two processes read the same old value and one write overwrites the other's update.
A two-process software critical-section protocol using per-process flags and a shared turn variable.
An atomic hardware instruction that returns the old value of a word and sets it to a new value.
A lock with acquire and release operations that has one owner at a time.
An integer accessed only by atomic wait and signal operations.
A semaphore whose value is only 0 or 1 and is often used like a mutex.
A semaphore that can take values above 1 and counts available resource units.
A lock whose waiting thread repeatedly tests the lock in a loop.
A synchronization construct that combines shared data and procedures with implicit mutual exclusion.
A monitor queue on which a process waits and is later signalled when a condition may be true.
A set of processes in which each process waits for a resource held by another process in the set.
A directed graph with process and resource nodes showing requests, assignments and releases.
A deadlock condition where a process holds one resource while waiting for another.
A deadlock condition where a resource cannot be forcibly taken from its holder.
A deadlock condition where a closed chain of processes each waits for a resource held by the next.
Indefinite postponement of a process even though deadlock may not exist.
A state in which at least one order exists for all processes to finish without deadlock.
A deadlock-avoidance algorithm that treats resources like loans and grants a request only if the state stays safe.
A runtime check that finds a cycle in a wait-for graph or a set of processes that cannot finish.
